title: How Long, O LORD?
subtitle: Habakkuk 1
description: Habakkuk complains about violence and broken courts in Judah, and God answers with the Chaldeans.
paragraphs: Most prophet books open with a king and a year. This one opens with a weight. What Habakkuk carries is “the burden that Habakkuk the prophet received in a vision”, and the book never dates it, never names the king on Judah's throne, never says where the prophet stood when it came. Its only clock is the trouble itself. Violence has filled the prophet's own nation, the courts have stopped working, and God has not answered. So the first words of the book are not a sermon. They are a complaint, filed by a man who has been praying into silence.

Habakkuk's complaint is about Judah, not about foreign enemies. “How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear”, he asks, or cry out “Violence!” and receive no rescue. The wrong is in front of him daily: “Why do You make me see iniquity? Why do You tolerate wrongdoing?” Destruction and violence stand before him, strife is ongoing, and conflict abounds, and the machinery that should stop it has seized. “Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth.” The reason is named plainly: “For the wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted.” The righteous are surrounded, the verdicts come out twisted, and heaven's silence is the prophet's first problem.

Then God answers, and the answer is not comfort. “Look at the nations and observe”, He says, “be utterly astounded!” What is coming will strain belief even when it is announced in advance: “For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe even if someone told you.” The work has a name, and the name is the worst nation on the horizon. “For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans”, God says, and the description that follows the dash is its own sentence: “that ruthless and impetuous nation which marches through the breadth of the earth to seize dwellings not their own.” Judah's violence will be answered by an invader whose whole business is taking houses that are not his.

God Himself draws the portrait of the army He is raising. They are dreaded and feared, a law to themselves, deriving their justice and sovereignty from no one above them. Their cavalry outruns animals: “Their horses are swifter than leopards, fiercer than wolves of the night.” They come from far off and drop on their prey like a vulture swooping down to devour. All of them come bent on violence, their hordes advance like the east wind, and they gather prisoners like sand. Kings are a joke to them and rulers an object of scorn. Every fortress makes them laugh; they pile up siege ramps and take it.

The portrait ends on the invader's religion, which is himself. Having swept by like the wind and passed through, he stands guilty before the God who raised him, though he does not know it: “They are guilty; their own strength is their god.” That is where the first movement of the book stops. Habakkuk asked how long God would tolerate violence in Judah, and God answered that He would not tolerate it much longer, that judgment was already on the road in the form of a nation worse than the one being judged. The silence is broken. What it says raises a harder question than the one the prophet asked, and Habakkuk is about to ask it.

title: Will He Continue to Slay Nations Without Mercy?
subtitle: Habakkuk 1
description: The prophet protests that a holy God is silent while the wicked swallow the righteous, then takes his post to wait.
paragraphs: Habakkuk does not flinch from the answer, but he does not accept it quietly either. He takes hold of who God is and argues from it. “Are You not from everlasting, O LORD, my God, my Holy One?” The everlasting God cannot be finished by His own judgment, and the prophet says so: “We will not die.” He grants the whole design before he protests it. “O LORD, You have appointed them to execute judgment; O Rock, You have established them for correction.” The Chaldeans are an appointment, not an accident. Correction is the purpose. It is the instrument that Habakkuk cannot reconcile with the hand holding it.

The protest is built on God's own character. “Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil, and You cannot tolerate wrongdoing.” A God like that, Habakkuk says, should not be able to watch this. “So why do You tolerate the faithless? Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?” The problem is no longer Judah's violence; Judah's violence at least explains a judgment. The problem is a holy God gone quiet while a faithless nation eats a nation less wicked than itself, and the prophet puts the contradiction to God directly, in God's own terms.

He pictures what the silence looks like from underneath. “You have made men like the fish of the sea, like creeping things that have no ruler.” Human beings reduced to fish in open water, no king over them, no protection, swimming in schools while something above them fishes. The foe pulls all of them up with a hook. He catches them in his dragnet and gathers them in his fishing net, and the catch makes him glad. Whole peoples come up in the mesh, and the fisherman does not thank God for the haul. He thanks the net.

That is the detail Habakkuk cannot get past. “Therefore he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net”, he says, because by these things the fisherman's portion is rich and his food is sumptuous. The conqueror worships his own tackle. His strength was already his god when God introduced him; now the net gets the incense too. And there is no sign in heaven that the fishing will ever be called to account. So the chapter's last line is a question aimed straight up: “Will he, therefore, empty his net and continue to slay nations without mercy?” If the net is never emptied of its catch and never stopped, the slaying simply goes on, nation after nation, forever.

Then Habakkuk does the most disciplined thing in the book. He stops talking and takes his post. “I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts.” Like a watchman on a city wall he will wait where waiting is the assignment. “I will watch to see what He will say to me, and how I should answer when corrected.” He expects an answer, and he expects the answer may correct him, the complainant, and he stations himself to receive both. The second complaint is on the record. The prophet is on the wall. The book holds its breath with him.

title: The Righteous Will Live by Faith
subtitle: Habakkuk 2
description: God commands the vision written on tablets: an appointed time, and the righteous living by faith.
paragraphs: The answer comes to the man on the ramparts, and its first instruction is about writing. “Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it.” The vision is not a private comfort for Habakkuk. It is to be cut into tablets plainly enough that a runner can carry it at speed and read as he goes. What God is about to say belongs to people who have not yet heard it, and it has to survive being transported. The prophet who complained twice is now a scribe with an assignment.

The vision also comes with a clock, and the clock is not Habakkuk's. “For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie.” The end it speaks of is fixed, but it is not near, and God says both things at once without softening either. “Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay.” Lingering and not delaying stand in the same sentence. From the wall where Habakkuk stands, the fulfillment will feel late. From the appointed time, it will arrive exactly when it was set. Waiting is not a gap in the plan. Waiting is the plan's appointed shape for the people who receive the vision.

Then the answer draws its line through the human race, in two fragments split by the text's own dashes. “Look at the proud one; his soul is not upright.” That is the first kind of person, swollen, crooked inside. Against him stands the second kind, in the sentence the whole book turns on: “the righteous will live by faith.” No armies are measured here, no calendars given. The proud man's soul is not upright, and the righteous man's life is carried by trusting. Between those two descriptions, everyone in the book has to be located, the Chaldean on his march and the prophet on his wall alike.

The proud one gets a fuller portrait, and it is the fisherman from the first complaint, seen now from God's side. “and wealth indeed betrays him”, the vision continues, running on from the sentence before it. “He is an arrogant man never at rest.” His appetite is the appetite of the grave: “He enlarges his appetite like Sheol, and like Death, he is never satisfied.” That is why the net never empties. “He gathers all the nations to himself and collects all the peoples as his own.” Death gathers everyone eventually and is never full, and the conqueror has made himself death's student, collecting peoples the way the grave collects bodies, and calling the collection glory.

So the answer to the second complaint is not an explanation of the silence. It is a written vision, an appointed time, and a distinction. God does not tell Habakkuk why the wicked may swallow the righteous for a season. He tells him the season has an end that is already scheduled, that the proud soul gathering nations is gathering its own betrayal with them, and that the righteous will live, in the meantime and at the end, by faith. The tablets are inscribed. What remains is to say what the gathered nations themselves will one day say, and the vision now puts words in their mouths.

title: Woe to Him Who Amasses What Is Not His
subtitle: Habakkuk 2
description: The plundered nations sing five woes over the conqueror, ending in the silence of the temple.
paragraphs: The vision now hands the conqueror over to his victims. “Will not all of these take up a taunt against him, speaking with mockery and derision”, and the taunt is a song of five woes that the plundered nations themselves will sing. The first woe is about debt run in reverse. “Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans!” The empire has been borrowing nations and calling the loans wealth, and the song asks how long it thinks that lasts. The answer is a morning surprise: “Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey.” And the arithmetic under it is exact: “the remnant of the people will plunder you”, because the plunderer is what he plundered others into being.

The second woe lands on the house the plunder built. “Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!” The nest on the cliff was supposed to be untouchable, dynasty secured above the reach of revenge. Instead the building itself testifies. He has plotted shame for his own house by cutting off many peoples, and the materials know it: “For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork.” A palace whose walls accuse the builder is not a fortress. It is evidence that has learned to talk.

The third woe widens from the house to the city. “Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!” Empires call this founding; the song calls it by its cost. And the LORD of Hosts Himself is behind the verdict that all that forced labor accomplishes nothing permanent: “the labor of the people only feeds the fire, and the nations weary themselves in vain.” Then, in the middle of the woe, the song opens a window onto the actual future of the earth. “For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.” Not the conqueror's glory. Not his name on the city. The earth is reserved for a different fame, total as seawater, and his blood-built town is a wearying of people for nothing.

The fourth woe is about the cup. “Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbors”, pouring from the wineskin until they are drunk, to gaze at their nakedness. Shame was his entertainment; nations were stripped for his amusement. The song turns the cup around. He will be filled with shame instead of glory, and he too must drink and be exposed. “The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you, and utter disgrace will cover your glory.” What he poured for others arrives in his own hand, measured by the same host. And the last woe addresses the god who could not answer any of this. “Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake!’ or to silent stone, ‘Arise!’” The image is overlaid with gold and silver, a teacher of lies, and for all its craftsmanship, “there is no breath in it at all.” The conqueror's strength was his god, and his god is a carved thing that cannot speak, cannot guide, cannot breathe.

After five woes, the taunt does not end with a shout. It ends with the opposite of one. “But the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him.” The carved gods cannot speak, and the living God does not need to compete with them. He is in His temple, and the appropriate response of the whole earth, conquerors and complainers together, is silence. The vision is complete: written, timed, and sung. What Habakkuk does with it is the book's last movement, and he does not argue anymore. He prays.

title: Yet I Will Rejoice in the LORD
subtitle: Habakkuk 3
description: Habakkuk prays: God comes in glory, the prophet trembles, and rejoices over empty fields.
paragraphs: The book's last chapter is not another oracle. It is “a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth”, a song with directions attached, meant to be sung by people who were not Habakkuk. It begins with a report received. “O LORD, I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds.” The prophet who demanded answers now asks for the deeds themselves, in his own generation: “Revive them in these years; make them known in these years.” And knowing what those years hold, because God has told him, he adds the plea the whole prayer balances on: “In Your wrath, remember mercy!”

Then the prayer sees God coming. “God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.” The prayer carries its own notation here, Selah, a marking woven through the song three times, and after it the scale widens: “His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth.” The radiance is physical. “His radiance was like the sunlight; rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden.” Plague went before Him and fever followed in His steps, the way an army's dust precedes it. “He stood and measured the earth; He looked and startled the nations”, and at the looking, the ancient mountains crumbled and the perpetual hills collapsed. Cushan's tents are in distress and Midian's curtains tremble, peoples shaking at a presence they can feel through cloth.

The prayer's questions are not complaints now; they are wonder at the old war stories. Was God angry at the rivers, wrathful at the streams, raging at the sea, when He rode His horses and His chariots of salvation? The bow comes out: God brandished it and called for many arrows, and “You split the earth with rivers.” Creation itself reacts in the telling. “The mountains saw You and quaked”, the deep roars with its voice and lifts its hands on high, and “Sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, at the brightness of Your shining spear.” Through it all the purpose is named once, plainly, in the middle of the storm: “You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed.” The head of the house of the wicked is crushed with his own spear, the warriors who stormed out to devour the weak in secret are scattered, and the sea is trampled under God's horses, churning the great waters.

Hearing all this does not steady the prophet's body. It undoes it. “I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound.” The decay is in his bones; he trembles where he stands. And the waiting the vision commanded is still his assignment, now with the invasion named as certain: “Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us.” The prayer is not denial. The day of distress is coming for his own nation first, he knows it, he believes the report, and his knees are shaking under the knowledge. Everything the book has built, two complaints, a vision, five woes, stands behind the sentence he says next.

He says it over an empty farm. “Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines”, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and there are no cattle in the stalls, an inventory of everything a household lives on, gone item by item, “yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!” The rejoicing is not because the fields recovered. They did not. It stands on the last line of the book: “GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights!” The man who began the book crying how long ends it on high ground with a deer's footing, still in the same trouble, carried by a different strength. And the prayer closes the way songs do, handed over for singing: “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments.”
